verdict.tagline: Brutal vengeance and rivalries shine despite clumsy controls and repetitive tasks.
for_you_if: you enjoy building personal rivalries with enemies
you want fluid combat drawing inspiration from classic action games
not_for_you_if: you need smooth keyboard and mouse movement
you want varied side quests and open-world activities

claims.claim: Reviewers highlight the Nemesis System as a standout, unique feature that creates personal rivalries and dynamic enemy interactions.

citations.review_text: I don’t really like The Lord of the Rings, or the Hobbit but Shadow of Mordor is an amazing game! The nemesis system is one of a kind! I had one orc that always got away or killed me and while it did anger me in so many ways it just made the thrill, chase and final kill at the very end of the game so much better and well earned!

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is a fun, stylish hack & slash that shines most when you’re carving through hordes of orcs. If you like the combat of the Batman: Arkham games and the traversal of Assassin’s Creed, this blends those ideas into a solid, easy-to-pick-up experience. The Nemesis System is the standout feature, adding personality and unpredictability to your enemies in a way that keeps things interesting. That said, the game does get repetitive, especially early on, and the world feels a bit limited with only two relatively small maps. It’s easy to burn through the main content quickly if you stay focused, and it can feel like it needed more depth and expansion overall. Still, it’s a lot of fun while it lasts, and watching your character grow stronger while taking on tougher orcs is genuinely satisfying. Not perfect, but definitely worth playing.
Nemesis system is one of the best gameplay mechanics ever made, Best lotr game yet.

Shadow of Mordor is fine, but not interesting enough for to justify playing more of. 

SoM plays like a pure power fantasy (similar to later Assassin's Creed games) where the point of the game is to rip through hordes of enemies as an overpowered main character, with a bit of plot laid on top to justify your crusade. This is fine if that's your thing, but I really didn't enjoy it due to the lack of challenge. The fights felt very... canned? After maybe half an hour I realized I didn't actually need skill to win fights. If I mashed attack, then hit the parry button when prompted, I could win most encounters. No creative movements, items, or approaches necessary. Enemies swarm around you, then do the action-movie-stunt-man thing of kinda waiting in the wings while I kill each of them 1v1. Even when you get close to death, the game goes slo-mo and gives you every opportunity to kill your attacker and get back on your feet. There was hardly any real danger., which would be less of a problem if essentially the whole focus of the game weren't "go to this place, kill this person."

The Nemesis System is also really cool (I'm not saying anything new here, this is what everyone recognizes), and I would really love to see it implemented in a game with combat and mechanics that I enjoy more. It's a great idea with tons of possibility for dynamic storytelling. The problem is that Warner Bros owns a patent on it until 2036, and hasn't made a game utilizing it in- at the time of this review- 9 years. So that sucks.

Oddly, I think this game would work much better as a roguelite. It's already repetitive enough that a run-based gameplay loop wouldn't feel out of place, and each boss you beat could come back in later runs with extra strength and malice due to your rivalry. Plus, it could give you the opportunity to become overpowered without basically starting off that way. Ah well, maybe in 2036.

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor is one of the few licensed games that feels confident enough to stand on its own. It does not rely only on the fame of Tolkien’s world; it builds a dark, brutal, and highly entertaining experience with its own identity. From the opening hours, the game throws you into a version of Mordor that feels hostile, cruel, and constantly alive, and that sense of danger makes every victory feel earned.

What makes the game immediately compelling is the flow of movement and combat. Traversing ruins, climbing towers, and leaping across the landscape feels smooth and satisfying, while the battles are aggressive without becoming messy. There is a strong sense of rhythm in every fight, and once the mechanics click, Talion becomes incredibly fun to control. The game makes you feel powerful, but never so safe that the tension disappears completely.

The true star of the experience, however, is the Nemesis system. That mechanic gives the game a personality most action titles can only dream of. Orc captains remember defeats, return with scars, rise through the ranks, mock you, ambush you, and turn simple encounters into personal grudges. Because of that, the world feels reactive in a way that still feels impressive. You are not just clearing icons on a map — you are creating rivalries and stories that feel strangely unique to your own playthrough.

Talion and Celebrimbor also make an effective pair at the center of the story. Their relationship gives the narrative a darker and more driven tone than a standard revenge plot. The game may not be the deepest story ever told in Middle-earth, but it understands how to keep the player invested through mystery, anger, and momentum. It gives just enough emotional weight to make the violence feel purposeful rather than empty.

What I appreciate most is how the game balances spectacle with player freedom. You can charge directly into a stronghold, stalk enemies from above, manipulate the hierarchy of the Uruks, or …

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the keyboard and mouse controls as awkward and clumsy, noting issues with mouse capture and movement bindings.

citations.review_text:
It's a controller game. Keyboard and mouse is an option only in name. The control scheme is awkward, the camera controls dreadful and the movement system clumsy beyond belief. The "sprint after landing" window is incredibly long. Also the window fails to actually capture the mouse (no matter the window setting), so I kept going over to my second monitor. 

The game continuously yells at you "HEY THIS IS A VIDEOGAME BTW", so there is absolutely no danger of any immersion. Few of the mechanics have any world/lore tie in, you collect points and "purchase" abilities. You get elf arrows from sucking off orcs and randomly in the environment.

The story setup is also weak, mostly due to how straightforward it is. It's such a cookie cutter setup. The elf you are soul bound to also gets no real introduction? He's just there, no "hello", no "who are you", nothing. The entire sequence feels like "ah damn we have to make a plot hook and tutorial, well whatever, just cobble something together". I will say the sneak tutorial being to kiss your wife is creative.

My introduction to the game proper was comical. A random troll immediately killed two captains which of course locks you into this wonderful sequence of "zoom into random orc, get pushed through a series of menus". Again, it's just all so clumsy.

The combat system sure is there and it sure is clumsy. It's also so mindless. It's the classic "enemies take turns attacking you". You also get callouts for every incoming attack, making the whole thing feel like a quick time event.

Every mechanic i encountered so far has been incredibly dumbed down and made ridiculously easy. The stealth is silly and the time windows for blocking  are about twice or thrice as long as they IMO should be.

One thing that did stand out to me, was how alive the world felt. There were always orcs running around, getting into fights or chasing after slaves.

I'm aware this is an old game and I am judging it harshly with modern day eyes, but witcher …

Movement controls ARE BONKERS for anyone used to PC gaming.

W / D actually rotate the player.... WTF that's what the mouse is for.

Weird camera angles too. Not sure if I am going to get very far, but keeping because I want to want to like it, and 3.99$USD is great.

Feels like this was a console port and designed with controller first mentality in mind.

The HD texture pack looks pretty good too.

Also, it works on LINUX so that's a plus.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that missions and combat loops become repetitive over time.

citations.review_text: The game is highly repetitive: fights play out the exact same way from the moment you install to the moment you decide to quit. There's no real room for growth tactically aside from just increasing the power of your character and the difficulty only goes downhill because next to no new mechanics are introduced as the game progresses

The game is extremely boring and repetitive, giving no sense of progress whatsoever.

The missions are boring. Take the Grog Poisoning mission, for instance, you have to dig for herbs in three different map locations, performing the exact same interactions many times . Then there's the explosive cargo escort mission where you need to destroy Sauron's statue. The variation is just clearing three separate locations of enemies.

The other quests feel like everything boils down to "kill X enemies using Y method." There's no depth, no meaningful progression. Combat is boring too, it feels like smashing the attack button until enemies die. The enemies for the most part don't give the feel that you are attacking them, it feels like the hero is slicing the air until you kick someone, but the kick just happens as you mash the attack button...

Character movement is very bad, it sticks to everything, so around ruins or other buildings you have little control over what the character is doing and it often doesn't behave in an intuitive manner.

The Nemesis system? It just exists. Every orc still feels interchangeable and the supposed "unique" rivalries mean nothing when the core loop stays identical throughout. The only difference is you sometimes get some sort of greeting and health bar above an enemy. Sometimes you have to check for weakpoints, but that doesn't change the feeling it is repetitive.

Is there something good?
If you want some really undemanding entertainment, you could just push forward in the direction where the game tells you the mission is and mash the attack button once you engage in combat.

[h2]Middle Earth: Shadow of the Bat[/h2]

A nice action experience, but gets old really fast and fails to be more than a platform to show off the nemesis system, which ends up being a crutch for the game. It is hard not to compare this game's combat to the successful Arkham City. 
But that is not a bad thing, because Arkham City manages to create a fun and fluid combat, which is something Shadow of Mordor also does. My problem is that while Arkham City is full of moments that break that non stop action with different kinds of challenges, Mordor does not evolve it's gameplay loop that much making the experience feel repetitive. The story also fails to give more substance to the experience, were any cutscene or dialogue feels like a real drag, followed by some variation of the same type of mission with a few exceptions. A good game, but a little half baked for my taste.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the final boss encounters and ending sequence as underwhelming or disappointing.

citations.review_text:
Grabbed this during a Steam sale after remembering I had played it on Xbox 360 years ago without ever finishing it. I’m not a huge Lord of the Rings fan, so I went in mostly for the gameplay, and honestly, it still holds up surprisingly well. Combat is simple, fast, and incredibly satisfying, constantly throwing huge groups of Orcs at you while gradually unlocking new abilities that keep fights fresh. The real reason to play, though, is the Nemesis System. It absolutely deserves the praise it gets. Orcs remember previous encounters, climb the ranks if they kill you, develop strengths and weaknesses, and create little personal rivalries that make every playthrough feel unique. It’s one of the coolest gameplay systems I’ve seen, and it’s a shame it never became an industry standard.

The story, unfortunately, never reaches the same heights. It starts with a solid revenge setup and has a few interesting reveals, but the ending and final boss are incredibly underwhelming. Visually, the game has aged better than I expected, with great art direction and impressive enemy variety. Overall, Shadow of Mordor is still an easy recommendation. The Nemesis System alone makes it worth playing, and it left me genuinely excited to jump into Shadow of War.

...And one last thing: Sméagol is absolutely insufferable.

Combat is flowing, brutal, and incredibly satisfying. There are so many different gameplay mechanics and variations you are constantly becoming stronger and more versatile. The nemesis system and the way captains and warchiefs operate, and the strongholds and other areas are fun to experience, especially with late game abilities. The story is decent, but nothing special. Controls can be janky at times, especially with climbing and controller combos. The final mission of the game is incredibly underwhelming after being hyped up for the whole game,  instead the final 2 fights are not really fights at all. Still a great game, and never got tired of progressing, even doing the trivial side missions and collectibles. Even with its cons, 7.5/10
8/10, overall game is good just the ending is a bit unsatisfying or rushed i would say specially the final 3 fights

Combat is sweet, story is there. Endless spawning enemies which make it feel like your deeds in the story line make no impact on the world as enemies are instantly replaces and no way so far that I know of to disable alarms in camps so you gotta kill the alarm guys or basically battle an entire army for quite a long time. Which again the good combat makes it pretty satisfying but it can drag after awhile if multiple captains and chiefs pause the battle to monologue... every...time... The staple of this game is the fluid combat (when not interrupted by monologues). Movement feels like the older and actually good creed games parkour feels very similar. Recc if its on sale for 70% or more. Main campaign is short and the hunting missions kind of suck but torvin is cool. I dont want to spoil anything but the ending of the game is LAME. So prepare for disappointment if you thought cool combat would carry to the final battles.
Not bad game but really easy to play, could have been harder. And the final boss fight? Its not even a boss fight just cutscene. Bad finale.

[h3] 📢 Verdict: GRAB [/h3]
[b]TLDR:[/b] A fun stealth-action game set in the LOTR universe. The main catch is the patented Nemesis system, which easily overcomes the somewhat clunky camera and controls.

[list]
[*] 🔄 [b]The Loop:[/b] 
The Nemesis system is absolute genius. It genuinely feels like you are waging a guerrilla war against a massive adversary. Gathering intelligence on your targets, such as learning target strengths and weaknesses, and manipulating rivalries makes planning your strikes deeply satisfying, especially once wraith skills let you turn enemies to your side. Combat is fluid and fun; it isn't overly difficult, but chaining combos, stuns, and finishers feels great.

[*] 🎨 [b]The Vibe:[/b] 
Visually, the game holds up remarkably well given its age, especially if you enable the free ultra HD textures DLC. The Lord of the Rings atmosphere is solid throughout, and Gollum has his classic, wonderfully punchable personality, which I definitely count as a thematic win. Audio also holds up, with an immersive soundtrack that just screams LOTR. 

[*] ⚙️ [b]The Friction:[/b] 
The default field of view and movement controls can feel awkward initially. It almost ruined the first hour or two for me, until the flow clicked. There are also a few dated quicktime events scattered around, but they aren't overly bothersome. Menus are straightforward and easy to navigate, without much clutter. The only annoying bit was how gathering collectibles or completing events would automatically open menus, but I can let that go. 

[*] 🌐 [b]The Ecosystem:[/b] 
It is a massive shame that the Nemesis system is patented now, as more games desperately need a mechanic like this. The only other series that comes to mind with a similar mechanic was Mercenaries, but that's even more dated now. Still, as a complete singleplayer package with HD upgrades, it remains a fantastic experience that holds up years later.
[/list]

Such an interesting game in an awesome setting that is completely sabotaged by some of the worst controls I've ever played in an Action game, like I had to Google to make sure I wasn't crazy.

The controls are unresponsive and buggy, "Press Space to Do Something" and you just roll forward despite standing still and looking at the thing, but it's literally almost every action. Brutal delay on so many actions and when you include the baffling decision of animation locks leads to an objectively sluggish experience.

This game literally puts 5 actions on the same keys, I'm not joking. Spacebar = Climbs, Sprints, Dodge Rolls, Jumps Over Enemies, and Leaps from Ledges, I'm probably forgetting some. (Edit, it's actually 6 actions, I forgot the Speed Boost Over Obstacles)

Add in other annoyances like Stealth being buggy, the occasional bonus objective failing or succeeding with improper conditions, some bad DLC, and the end result is a frustrating experience.

I'd say worth it on a sale just because LOTR and the Nemesis system are so good, combat can be fun but you'll literally struggle more with the unresponsiveness of the controls than any actual gameplay which is generally quite easy.
With 8 hours playtime I didnt see any changes in gameplay. LMB spam or boring stealth / enviroment gameplay with MOST clunky movement and parkout ever

The open world is ugly and the missions are repetitive. The Nemesis system is overhyped and ultimately doesn't have a lot of mechanical or gameplay implications. Mechanics are [strike]stolen from[/strike] inspired by the Arkham Asylum and Assassin Creed games, which is an inspired combination, but they are executed worse; Talion often hits guys you don't want him to hit and climbs walls you don't want him to climb. The voice acting is incredible but is wasted on the bland dialogue and poorly-realized characters. The concept of a ranger being soul-melded with an elven wraith is super neat but isn't explored to it's full potential; these guys will go hours in-game without talking to each other, let alone bouncing off each other or shaping each other. The kill animations are very satisfying but as mentioned above the combat itself doesn't flow well.

Maybe this was impressive for its time but in 2026 it's a slog and I won't be finishing it.

citations.review_text:
I want so badly to recommend this game.... it just fails at so many things and it's so incredibly clunky, that I cannot in good conscience do it.

I will save my biggest issue with the game for last, as it's a gameplay mechanic spoiler, and I want to give people the opportunity to not read what they might consider a spoiler. So when you see the word "SPOILER!" and you don't want gameplay mechanic spoilers. Stop. I will not however spoil story.

First issue, there are no difficulty options. So if you find it too easy, or too hard, you cannot change that. What you see is what you get, one size fits all, like a ring that fits a hobbit, a human and a dark lord, as well as it fits a gollum. Whether it's comfortable for you or not.
Personally, I would've made the main game harder. But the DLC easier. More on that later.

Additionally, accessibility is abysmal. You have to hold to sprint, hold to sneak, and additionally press other buttons while holding both of those, and moving, to get stealth attacks... You have to sprint sneak, move, obviously, and stab. I find this difficult, I can't imagine how disabled gamers will ever do it without tools to aid them. I used to have a friend who managed to play Elden Ring, with a laptop track pad and an onsceen keyboard. So the adaptability of disabled gamers is amazing sometimes.... But it'd be nice if games wouldn't try and be a challenge for them. They should be able to play without having to out maneuver the game.

Additionally, Talion gets stuck... a lot. Chasing an orc? No can do, he runs as fast as you can, you're out of arrows and there's a single wall in the way.... Talion has decided to sneak against the wall, nope he's climbing and dangling off it, nope he's not climbing all the way down, oh, he's peaking round the wall now... TALION JUST GO AROUND THE WALL YOU ARSEHOLE!

The orcs are ANNOYING. Picture it, you're in the middle of some high octane action, you're slashing through orcs, you're beheading, you're running around…

I write bigger reviews on my website: https://therausereviews.substack.com/?utm_campaign=profile_chips
This is just a small one for steam

This game is extremely mediocre. The nemesis system is fantastic, and provides a super memorable set of enemies creating a satisfying playthrough loop. Where this game falters is everything surrounding it. The combat can be very clunky, same for platforming. I enjoyed the smaller nature of the map, but the lack of eye grabbing set pieces made it feel samey for the most part. The story, especially the ending, was a super large let down and made the game feel more like a prologue demo for the next game than its own product. I wish steam had a "meh" recommendation for games like this.

Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor — A Tech Demo Disguised as a Masterpiece
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I like this game—hell, I even love it a little. It is not a bad game; it is actually a good one. However, I have to push back against the overwhelming praise it has received over the years. Don’t be suckered in by the glowing word of mouth. On paper, it sounds incredible: Batman: Arkham combat mixed with Assassin’s Creed parkour, set in an open-world Lord of the Rings setting, all tied together by an innovative "Nemesis System." It sounds like the greatest game of all time, right? Wrong. It is all sorta BS—a classic case of a game being far less than the sum of its parts. To me, this felt less like a cohesive masterpiece and more like a tech demo for Monolith’s LithTech engine, designed to show publishers: "Look what our technology can do... please fund our next project."


🏃‍♂️ Clunky Movement & Rough Parkour
The parkour is incredibly rough. It reminds me of the first Assassin’s Creed, where you’d run up the corner of a building and slide right back down because you didn't approach it from the perfect angle.

Invisible Hitboxes: The collision geometry is constantly frustrating. You will find wide-open gaps you can't run through because a nearby log has an invisible hitbox larger than the object itself.

Dead Ends: Unclimbable mountains and walls are scattered everywhere.

Environmental Traps: In practice, the movement is clunky. You will likely get killed simply because your character locks up and gets stuck on the environment. Want to hang off a ledge to hide.. well good luck the game often decides to make you hang off the opposite ledge. Want to seamlessly bound from one roof to the next? Often there is no conective tissue between these roofs and ledges.. so you just fall all the way to the ground and have to climb back up instead of seamlessly leaping from roof top to roof top.. want to go left.. your character go…

Really fun game overall - definitely a bit clunky sometimes, but it's an older title, so I give it a pass. But it's a fun "what if" game in the world of Middle-Earth. 

The duality of the character gives to fun combat and an interesting story. I played the main game and started the Bright Lord DLC, was cool to see the backstory, but it felt too repetitive from the main game. Not bad, just felt like I was doing the same things again. I might come back and finish it, though.

citations.review_text:
I love it, however, it is quite repetitive in terms of side quests but the bonuses do make a difference. The story is well put, it does gave me the "scary" in crossing other characters, but overall the game is not really difficult in fighting against bosses because of how powerful the abilities that your character will have. 

From my experience, making an army to kill the chiefs and whatnot made it so easy because they can indeed get the job done while you are there jumping and waiting for them to kill it for you. Finally, the game is immersive and fun to play, I would recommend it. Note: I bought this at a discount, so I would also recommend to wait for the discount because it is a great deal.

Good game, if you want to be complenist for this game, it's gonna be punishing, some achievement is gonna pull your hair to complete it. LOL. 
The story was good, but the gameplay was repetitive at the end if you were gonna collect side items or do challenges like Ubisoft games a.k.a Assassins Creed.  
The DLC Bright Lord is more repetitive to complete just slightly different mission to mission: Capture tower, kill captains, do challenge, etc. At least the Hunting DLC is more fun than that.  
I recommend this for the story, and don't play this game in one sitting.

I can’t believe this game is already 11 years old, it still feels fresh in many ways. I had a great time playing it, even though there were moments when the gameplay loop felt a bit repetitive. What really stood out was how every encounter with an Orc captain or Warchief felt personal and unique, thanks to the Nemesis System. It gave each battle depth and made victories or defeats memorable.

The story itself is on the shorter side, but exploring the world and hunting down every artifact and Ithildin was surprisingly rewarding. Collecting these pieces added layers of lore and gave me reasons to keep diving back into Mordor. Between the main campaign and all the side content, there are easily hundreds of hours of gameplay to sink into if you enjoy completionist runs.

Overall, Shadow of Mordor is a very enjoyable and fun experience. It combines satisfying combat, a unique enemy system, and rich exploration. Even with its flaws, I’d definitely recommend giving it a try. it’s a game worth experiencing.

pros:
- the nemesis system (although it's not "100% polished" here yet. the better version is in the sequel)
- interesting narration around the player's deaths and resurrections, instead of just "you died, but let's pretend it never happened and reload the last checkpoint"

cons:
- half of the story takes place around the black gate, which is a very gloomy, uninteresting, same-looking-everywhere location in the whole LotR universe
- climbing towers to unlock warp points. not a bad format, but it's super repetitive and boring. compare it to Zelda BotW/TotK, where each tower has some variation. for example, some can't be climbed directly and require gliding from a nearby mountain, while others require digging underground and entering from below
- pressing two buttons on the gamepad at the same time. if only the (Y)+(B) combination existed, it'd be okay, but implementing all 4 combinations is too much. this also needs a larger input window, since the game often interprets the input as an isolated (Y) or (B) press instead
- irl legal aspect of the nemesis system prevented other games from using this cool mechanic, yet the studio abandoned it after only 2 games

A little janky due to its age, but an excellent game. So fun to run around the Black Gate and explore more of the interior of Mordor in a way you wouldn't really expect. Great story and memorable characters with such fun combat, akin to the Batman Arkham games. Feels like a mix of Assassin's Creed and Arkham in the best way. The Nemesis system is very cool also and not overdone like in the sequel. Biggest gripe was the ending contains a QTE for the final fight... Like... C'mon man. Also Sméagol is there. I guess.

claims.claim: Reviewers point out that enemy captains and warchiefs feature introductory cutscenes that play upon encounters.

citations.review_text:
I think that, considering this game's price, it's very easy to recommend to at least buy it and give it a go (especially if you get the bundle with Shadow Of War, which, whilst I haven't played that yet/will get to it next, I presume it's a much better version of this game). The story and characters are all really bad, and all of the villains, Sauron included, suck (except for Sauron's design), but perhaps it isn't helped that I don't like LOTR one bit. Nevertheless, the gameplay is pretty good! It's basically the Arkham free-flow combat with some tweaks and new moves, and it's quite enjoyable. However, the nemesis system (at least in this game/I haven't played War) sucks and is overrated. You don't really get to build stories or do anything with it unless you somehow die, but you're really overpowered in this game so that's going to be rare (and even then, it changes nothing and all of the enemies just have forced weaknesses you have to take advantage of in some cases else you can't even damage them, which is just unfun and forced). 

Additionally, it is the most tedious thing as to how every single time you meet a new captain, war chief, etc., that dumb cutscene introducing them plays. Perhaps for the first few it's fine, but it gets really annoying afterwards, especially if you're going for all of the achievements. Lastly, then, in relation to the achievements, the final "Mistress" one sucks; it's very RNG dependant and, as mentioned, annoying as hell because every second orc screams his introduction. Nevertheless, this is an average-mediocre game that I'd suggest playing when it's on sale at 90% off with War also.
It's fun enough. The introduction of captains get old after a bit, but anyway...

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as lacking any difficulty options to change the challenge level.

citations.review_text:
I want so badly to recommend this game.... it just fails at so many things and it's so incredibly clunky, that I cannot in good conscience do it.

I will save my biggest issue with the game for last, as it's a gameplay mechanic spoiler, and I want to give people the opportunity to not read what they might consider a spoiler. So when you see the word "SPOILER!" and you don't want gameplay mechanic spoilers. Stop. I will not however spoil story.

First issue, there are no difficulty options. So if you find it too easy, or too hard, you cannot change that. What you see is what you get, one size fits all, like a ring that fits a hobbit, a human and a dark lord, as well as it fits a gollum. Whether it's comfortable for you or not.
Personally, I would've made the main game harder. But the DLC easier. More on that later.

Additionally, accessibility is abysmal. You have to hold to sprint, hold to sneak, and additionally press other buttons while holding both of those, and moving, to get stealth attacks... You have to sprint sneak, move, obviously, and stab. I find this difficult, I can't imagine how disabled gamers will ever do it without tools to aid them. I used to have a friend who managed to play Elden Ring, with a laptop track pad and an onsceen keyboard. So the adaptability of disabled gamers is amazing sometimes.... But it'd be nice if games wouldn't try and be a challenge for them. They should be able to play without having to out maneuver the game.

Additionally, Talion gets stuck... a lot. Chasing an orc? No can do, he runs as fast as you can, you're out of arrows and there's a single wall in the way.... Talion has decided to sneak against the wall, nope he's climbing and dangling off it, nope he's not climbing all the way down, oh, he's peaking round the wall now... TALION JUST GO AROUND THE WALL YOU ARSEHOLE!

The orcs are ANNOYING. Picture it, you're in the middle of some high octane action, you're slashing through orcs, you're beheading, you're running around…

I wish the main campaign was longer but there is endless replayability with the "trials of war". 

The combat is like a mix of sleeping dogs and Arkham but is slightly easier than both those games. I wish it had difficulty settings to make the orc encounters a bit harder, after like 15h of gameplay you get good enough to not feel the benefits of the nemesis system without purposely losing to a couple orcs. 

One of my favourite games of all time. Absolute power trip to just power up and slash the shrakh out of all the orcs! 

Wait for a sale and get the middle earth shadow bundle for $6.99. Easy 100+ hours of orc murder fun

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the game requires holding multiple buttons simultaneously for movement and stealth actions, which can be difficult to execute.

pros:
- the nemesis system (although it's not "100% polished" here yet. the better version is in the sequel)
- interesting narration around the player's deaths and resurrections, instead of just "you died, but let's pretend it never happened and reload the last checkpoint"

cons:
- half of the story takes place around the black gate, which is a very gloomy, uninteresting, same-looking-everywhere location in the whole LotR universe
- climbing towers to unlock warp points. not a bad format, but it's super repetitive and boring. compare it to Zelda BotW/TotK, where each tower has some variation. for example, some can't be climbed directly and require gliding from a nearby mountain, while others require digging underground and entering from below
- pressing two buttons on the gamepad at the same time. if only the (Y)+(B) combination existed, it'd be okay, but implementing all 4 combinations is too much. this also needs a larger input window, since the game often interprets the input as an isolated (Y) or (B) press instead
- irl legal aspect of the nemesis system prevented other games from using this cool mechanic, yet the studio abandoned it after only 2 games
